title: This Fake YouTuber Ad Almost Took My Dad's Savings
creator: Nadia Hussain
description:
My dad nearly sent money to a crypto platform that doesn't exist, after watching a deepfake video of a creator he trusts. I'm walking through the exact script so you can spot the next one.

QuantumYield is not a real company. Do not search for it, do not go to any site using that name.

If you've been scammed: report it to your bank first, then to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

sentences.t: Two weeks ago my dad called me, really excited, and asked if I'd heard of a trading app called QuantumYield.
He'd seen a video from a finance creator he watches every week, and he was about to put in five thousand dollars.
The thing is, that creator never made that video, it was a deepfake, and QuantumYield doesn't exist.
So today I'm going to read you the exact script from the fake, because once you hear it, you'll recognize the next one.
Okay, here's what the fake version of him says, word for word, I transcribed it from my dad's phone.
Hey everyone, this video is brought to you by QuantumYield, the AI trading platform that made my viewers forty thousand dollars last month.
Just sign up at quantumyield dot io slash vip and use code GOLD for a free bonus on your first deposit.
But hurry, this offer is only for the first hundred people, and spots are almost gone.
That's it, that's the whole thing, and if you didn't know better, it sounds exactly like a normal sponsor read.
And that is the point, the scammers copy the shape of a real ad on purpose, because we've all learned to trust that shape.
So let's go through the red flags, because there are a lot of them once you slow down.
Number one, the promise, forty thousand dollars last month.
No real sponsor is allowed to promise you returns, that's not a marketing choice, it's against the law in most countries.
Number two, the urgency, first hundred people, spots almost gone.
Real companies want as many customers as possible, they're not going to close the door after a hundred.
Number three, the face, and this one is harder.
If you watch closely, his mouth doesn't quite match on words with a B or an M, it kind of smears.
And he never turns his head, the whole clip, he's perfectly front on, like a passport photo.
Number four, where it showed up, which was an ad on a social feed, not on his actual channel.
If a creator really has a sponsor, it's in their real videos, on their real channel, and you can go check.
My dad didn't check, and honestly, why would he, he's seen that man's face every Sunday for three years.
And number five, the domain, which had been registered eleven days before he saw the ad.
You can look that up for free, and anything handling your money that's younger than a carton of milk, run.
So what did we actually do?
We called his bank together, and luckily he hadn't sent anything yet, he'd only made an account.
We changed the password he'd reused on that site, because of course he'd reused it, everyone's dad reuses it.
We reported the ad on the platform, and we reported the site, and I emailed the real creator, who was horrified.
He's since made a video warning his own viewers, which is how I know for sure it wasn't him.
Please send this to your parents, your grandparents, anyone who watches finance videos and trusts the faces in them.
And if it's already happened to someone you love, they're not stupid, these things are built by professionals.
Take care of each other, I'll see you next time.
